Tomas

Pip cracks the Gale Bomb against the cobbles. For one second, in a city where the air has not moved in forty years — there is wind.
The kite leaps out of Tomas's hands and goes up, and up, red against the white sky.
IT'S FLYING! IT'S FLYING!
All around the garden, the frozen festival-goers turn their heads, very slowly, to watch it. One of them laughs. A real laugh. It sounds rusty.

Dead Man's Hand
Lucky Sel
Blank. Forty years, and they were blank.
Funny. I feel lighter.
Lucky Sel has held "the best hand of his life" for forty years without playing it. Corvin wants a word.
Pull up a chair, friend. I'm holding the best hand of my life. Been holding it since lunch.
Since lunch forty years ago. You never played it?
Never had to. As long as I hold it, it's the best hand of my life. Play it, and it's just a hand.
Sparrow, hold my hat. This one's personal.
Raise.
Call.
Fold.

I'll see that, and raise forever. Again?

Sel lays his cards down, one by one. They are blank. All five. Not a mark on them.

Corvin called a forty-year bluff in a tavern in Evernoon. The cards were blank. He looked happier than I've ever seen him.
Scraped Knee
Mother Dawe

Please, take this. My mother wore it in the Thornwood. Moss grows back over anything, she used to say.
That's how it's supposed to work. It hurts, and then it stops. Nobody here remembers the second part.
Ilse cleaned a scraped knee that had been bleeding, painlessly, for forty years. The girl cried, and then she stopped. Ilse called it the best surgery of her career.
She's off playing again. Falling over, getting up. Isn't that marvelous?
